title: Human-readable repositories: structuring a repository for people

sections.name: claim
sections.label: Claim
sections.content: How an SRS repository is structured so a person or a cold agent can read it: find a top-level introduction, then drill down into parts. The owner, 2026-10-26: "A srs repository should have a structure that makes sense to browse"; 2026-10-30: research "should be structured as a tree of documents that get deeper".

sections.name: story
sections.label: The story so far
sections.content: The spec decided the skeleton: a required root container whose identity is the repository's purpose (RFC-013), and an ordered outline whose order is the navigation (RFC-043). It never decided the front door, and the tools do not yet honour the order. The practice ran ahead of the spec: srs-context reads in numbered layers, muSrs is being regrouped into areas, and LiveWyer Insight showed that a third-party repository can read well with today's tools. This Research section is built the same way: introduction, thread overview, parts, evidence.

sections.name: parts
sections.label: The parts
sections.content:
1. The front door: what a repository opens on.
2. Reading order and sections: a few areas, then deeper.
3. Labels, headings and reading views.
4. Structure that stays stable as it grows.
5. How we know a repository reads well.
Each part states its principle and whether it is decided, practised or proposed.

sections.name: open
sections.label: Open questions
sections.content: What the front door is in the spec. Who decides the top-level areas, and how purpose becomes structure. How a structural change is recorded. Whether navigation depth comes from the contains tree or container outlines, and whether that can be one way.
